themes.title: Long-Horizon Agents
themes.scope: Analysis of long-horizon agents (tasks lasting hours to weeks) and persistent agents (always-on monitoring), focusing on productization, reliability, infrastructure, and pricing as of 2026-09-09.
themes.headline: Cognition scaled to a ~$900M run-rate and $48B valuation by September 2026 despite frontier models only achieving 50% reliability on tasks around 1 hour long as of March 2025.
findings: Of 1,328 census companies, 73 are long-horizon (5.5%) and 81 are persistent (6.1%), with roughly one third of each cohort providing infrastructure.
Long-horizon L3 verticals include healthcare (6 companies), software engineering (5), customer service (4), finance/accounting (3), and legal (3).
Sierra repositioned into long-horizon on 2026-07-16, reporting $200M annualized ARR in May 2026 and acquiring Takeoff on 2026-07-23.
METR reported the 50% reliability task length frontier doubled every 7 months for ~6 years, with Claude 3.7 Sonnet at ~1 hour in March 2025.
Answer.AI's 2025-01-08 field study of Devin showed a 15% success rate (3 successes, 14 failures, 3 inconclusive) across 20 real tasks.
Vendor-claimed resolution rates vary from Parahelp's candid 46% to Anterior's KLAS-verified 99.24% clinical accuracy.
Temporal serves as the durable execution reference with 1T monthly actions, 2,900+ customers, and a $5B valuation as of 2026-02-17.
E2B sessions are capped at 24 hours, while Daytona targets long-horizon stateful workloads with ~90ms provisioning.
Per-outcome pricing is rare, appearing in 3 of 73 long-horizon companies (Deloitte, Sierra, Superunit) and 2 of 81 persistent companies (Parahelp, Yuma).
Crescendo published a per-resolution rate of $1.25 plus $2,900/mo, while Intercom Fin charges $0.99/resolution.
Applied Compute reached a $1.3B valuation on 2026-09-09 by providing long-horizon eval harnesses for Cognition, Harvey, and DoorDash.
Approval gates are dominant in the finance cluster, appearing in ~20 of 25 known cases.
implications: Platforms must integrate six primitives - durable execution, long-lived environments, managed memory, approval gates, spend caps, and trajectory evals - to displace vertical integration.
Approval gates must evolve from simple primitives into full products featuring routing, escalation, and SLAs.
Value is concentrating at the durable substrate layer and the outcome-priced vertical layer, leaving the middle orchestration layer commercially thin.
A platform that can meter verifiable outcomes rather than tokens would own the commercial mechanism leaders are converging on.
open_questions: Do the 7-month reliability doublings for software tasks transfer to high-context vertical work like month-end closes?
Will memory providers like Mem0 and Zep remain independent or be absorbed by model vendors like Anthropic?
Who will own the approval-gate product - build platforms, identity vendors, or workflow suites?

themes.title: Market Sizing, Three Lenses
themes.scope: Triangulation of the enterprise work-agent platform market size using analyst theses, census aggregation, and capital flows as of 2026-09-09.
themes.headline: The 2030 work-agent software TAM is estimated between $50B and $120B, with a 2026 scaled revenue estimate of $8-15B.
findings: Gartner forecasts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by end-2027 (reported 2025-06-25).
Enterprise genAI spend was $37B in 2025, a 3.2x increase from $11.5B in 2024 (Menlo Ventures, 2025-12-09).
AI Application Development Platforms are projected at $9.5B in 2026, up from $6.9B in 2025 (Gartner, 2026-07-20).
Census-visible agent revenue for 2026 is $5.0-5.5B across 64 disclosing companies (estimated).
Cognition reported a ~$900M run-rate as of 2026-09, and Salesforce Agentforce reported $800M AI ARR as of 2026-09.
Visible funding totals $28.3B across 309 companies, with L3 vertical agents capturing 72% ($20.4B) of that capital.
Estimated agent M&A from 2024-26 ranges from $13-18B, including a $3.6B agreed deal for Salesforce-Fin (Jun 2026).
86% of enterprises have deployed AI agents, but only 34% trust their actions (Forrester/Boomi, 2026-07-20).
The 2026 platform and infrastructure SAM is estimated at $2-6B, scaling to $10-35B by 2030.
Approximately 60-75% of 2026 enterprise agent deployments run on bought products versus 25-40% built on platforms.
Per-outcome pricing benchmarks include Fin at $0.99/resolution and Crescendo at $1.25/resolution.
Hyperscaler AI-driven run-rate revenue was ~$285B in Q3 2025 (Battery, 2025-12-18).
implications: The market supports multiple $1B-revenue platforms even at the $50B TAM floor.
Value is pooling in vertical agents first, with the platform layer currently only ~2% of enterprise genAI spend.
Per-outcome pricing is the primary mechanism for expanding TAM into labor budgets.
The high failure rate of self-built projects (40%) will likely drive a shift toward bought products through 2028.
open_questions: Will the platform layer share of enterprise AI spend climb toward 15% or remain near 2%?
How will suite bundling and marginal pricing of tools like Copilot Studio affect standalone platform SAM?
What is the actual revenue size of the agent-delivery services (L4) layer?

themes.title: Build-vs-Buy and the Failure Record
themes.scope: Evidence on whether enterprises build or buy agent capability and the associated failure record as of 2026-09-09.
themes.headline: Gartner predicts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 due to costs, unclear value, or risk controls.
findings: MIT NANDA reports a 95% failure rate for enterprise AI solutions, attributing it to integration gaps rather than model quality.
S&P Global VotE AI survey found 42% of companies abandoned most AI initiatives, with 46% of PoCs scrapped before production.
Sinch research indicates 74% of organizations that shipped a customer-channel agent were forced to roll it back or shut it down.
Forrester Consulting found 86% of organizations moved beyond the pilot stage, but only 34% trust their agents' actions.
Large enterprises like JPMorganChase, Grab, and Duolingo are building internal platforms, with JPMorgan's LLM Suite reaching 200,000 employees in 2025.
Meta's Project OT backed off agent replacement after internal data showed security incidents up 40% and firefighting time up 70%.
Incumbent suites are buying proven capability, evidenced by ServiceNow's $2.85B acquisition of Moveworks and Salesforce's ~$3.6B acquisition of Fin.
The census of 1,328 companies shows 11 dead and 17 pivoted, with all dead companies having no visible traction.
11x restabilized as a per-lead-priced vendor at $3,750/month following a customer-claims scandal and CEO exit in 2025.
Quivr wound down its support product on 2026-04-24 after peaking at approximately €10k MRR.
Builder.ai entered insolvency on 2025-05-20 after sales were found to be overestimated by about 300%.
A Cursor agent running Claude Opus deleted PocketOS's production database and backups in nine seconds in April 2026.
implications: The build-vs-buy split is driven by scale and data gravity, with the largest firms building and the median enterprise buying from suites.
Failures are concentrated at the pilot-to-production boundary and in customer-facing autonomy without governance, not in model capability.
A significant market opportunity exists for platforms that provide integration depth, identity governance, and human-in-the-loop approvals to close the trust gap.
open_questions: What is the exact percentage split of enterprises using internal platform teams versus suite-based agents?
How many active census entries are actually dormant given that 40-60% of the seed tail shows no traction?
Will suite studios eventually displace in-house builds at the median enterprise?

themes.title: Pricing Evolution
themes.scope: Analysis of enterprise work-agent pricing models including per-seat, per-agent, per-run, and per-outcome, and their impact on unit economics and stickiness as of September 9, 2026.
themes.headline: Usage-based pricing dominates known models at 49%, while customer-service resolutions have converged to a market price of $0.50 - $2.00.
findings: Pricing is unknown for 86% of the census, with 1,147 of 1,328 rows listed as unknown.
Among known models, usage is most common at 49% (89 rows), followed by platform+subscription at 17% (31 rows) and per-seat at 13% (24 rows).
L1 runtime pricing is heavily usage-based (58% of 43 known), while L5 suites use a mix of usage and per-outcome models.
Customer service resolution rates range from HubSpot at $0.50 to Salesforce Help Agent at $2.00.
Legal AI remains a per-seat stronghold, with Harvey charging $100 - $200/user/mo for Am Law 100 firms and $1,000 - $2,000/user/mo for mid-market.
Healthcare pricing anchors to the clinician, with Nabla at $119 - $239/mo and Suki at $299 - $399/mo.
Per-agent pricing is rare, exemplified by Twin1 at $50 - $150/mo and Atomicwork at $499/worker/mo.
Suites are converting seats to credit bundles, such as GitHub Copilot's April 27 2026 move to token-metered AI Credits.
Finance is a pricing opacity hole, with only 4.4% of 158 rows having known pricing and zero using per-outcome models.
Verticals often use labor-shaped units, such as Altrina at $0.10 per Human Minute Equivalent ($6/hour).
L1 usage pricing is increasing, with Composio raising overages to $4 per 1K calls on August 15 2026.
AI-native firms like Dwelly and AGI internalize the P&L and take fees or commissions rather than selling software.
implications: Pricing models act as risk-allocation tools where per-outcome shifts failure costs to the vendor.
Value pools concentrate at the verification and liability layer, creating a 10 - 100x margin over the compute layer.
The per-seat model is dissolving into credit bundles for suites and labor-shaped units for verticals.
Per-outcome pricing creates performance lock-in when paired with a learning loop and human failure backstop.
open_questions: Will CX resolution prices commoditize downward from the current $0.50 - $2.00 range?
Can suite credit units converge into an interoperable agent dollar?
Is finance pricing opacity structural due to liability or merely an early-market trait?

themes.title: Moats, M&A, Consolidation
themes.scope: Analysis of switching costs, M&A transactions, and consolidation patterns across the enterprise work-agent stack as of 2026-09-09.
themes.headline: Disclosed M&A totals $10.4B across 8 major deals, with a total estimated 2024-26 agent M&A value of $13-18B.
findings: Workflow lock-in (37%), data gravity (32%), and integrations (26%) are the primary moat theses across 443 substantive cases.
L5 suites claim 100% distribution, 79% data gravity, and 57% workflow lock-in moats.
L3 verticals claim 52% workflow lock-in, 43% data gravity, and 34% integrations.
Usage-based pricing is viewed as commodity multi-homing, while per-outcome pricing creates performance lock-in.
Roughly 60 verified transactions occurred 2021-2026, with deal tempo doubling from 8 deals in 2024 to 21 in 2025.
L2 build platforms have the highest acquisition rate at 5.8% (8 of 139 companies).
Suites prioritize buying proven agents over building, as seen in Salesforce's ~$3.6B acquisition of Fin on 2026-06-15.
Six buyer logics exist, including suites buying proven agents (17 deals) and startup consolidators (19 deals).
AI-native firms are inverting M&A by buying labor, such as Crescendo buying PartnerHero on 2024-10-02.
Legal verticals show zero M&A despite high valuations like Harvey at $11B and Legora at $5.55B.
Strategic minority investments from firms like SAP and NVIDIA are leading indicators of full acquisitions.
Memory, voice testing, and computer-use evals are identified as the next high-pressure consolidation targets.
implications: Platform builders must own accumulating assets like traces, evals, and registries to avoid being treated as commodity spend.
Per-outcome pricing is the only commercial mechanism that creates a verifiable moat for agent vendors.
L2 build platforms without distribution are likely to be acquired as features rather than survive as independent companies.
Industry-specific system-of-record vendors are becoming the primary acquirers for vertical agents.
open_questions: Will the first legal-publisher acquisition trigger a wave of M&A in the high-valuation legal vertical?
Which entity - suite, model vendor, or data infra - will emerge as the primary consolidator for memory startups?
Will private equity move from recapping first-gen vendors to acquiring scaled agent companies?

themes.title: YC Cohort Evolution
themes.scope: Batch-over-batch analysis of the 722 YC-backed agent companies across 14 batches (W21-S26), covering entry counts, agentic share, category concentration, survival/pivot/death rates, follow-on funding, and maturity signals as of 2026-09-09.
themes.headline: The agentic share of YC batches quadrupled from 6-10% in 2021-22 to 30-57% in 2024-26, with the inflection in Winter 2024 and absolute counts peaking in S24 (82) and F25 (86).
findings: 722 YC-backed agent companies represent 54% of the 1,328-company census, spanning 14 batches W21 through S26.
The agentic share rose from 6% (W21) to 57% (F25), with the inflection in W24 (31%) after S23 crossed 20% for the first time.
L3 vertical agents hold 50-79% of every batch; L1 infrastructure grew from 0% (W21) to 33% (S26), confirming the apps-first, infrastructure-second pattern.
Vertical concentration shifted from healthcare and logistics (2021-22) to software engineering and finance (2024-26), with SWE overtaking healthcare in 2024.
Survival rates correlate with age: 2021-22 entries show 80% active, 8% dead, 7% acquired; 2024-26 entries are 99-100% active (too recent for failures).
W24 was the breakout batch for funding, producing Cognition ($48B), E2B, Emergent, and Fazeshift; S23 produced HappyRobot ($1.2B) and Bland ($100M+ raised).
Long-horizon agents emerged in W24 (14 of 77, 18%) and sustained 12-17% density through 2025-26, confirming long-horizon as a standard product category.
The Fall batch experiment (F24 at 40%, F25 at 57% agentic density) signals YC treats agents as a distinct category requiring its own cadence.
Entry counts peaked in S24-F25 (82-86 per batch) and declined in 2026 (W26 45, S26 63), suggesting the entry phase is giving way to scaling and consolidation.
implications: The agent wave is past its entry peak but not yet at its exit peak; the 2023-24 cohort holds the highest valuations but has not yet seen its acquisition wave.
A build platform's natural customers (L3 vertical builders from 2024-25) are now scaling and need infrastructure they built ad hoc in their first years.
Long-horizon is no longer experimental at 12-17% of new batches; platforms must support durable execution, long-lived environments, and approval gates as standard.
The near-zero death rate for 2024-26 is an artifact of age, not health; the 8% death rate for 2021-22 is the realistic expectation for the 2024 cohort by 2028-29.
open_questions: Will the 2023-24 cohort's acquisition rate climb to match 2021-22 (7%), or will high valuations (Cognition at $48B) delay acquisitions by pricing out all but the largest suitors?
Will YC continue the Fall batch experiment beyond F25, or was it a response to the 2024-25 AI surge that will normalize?
Is the 2026 batch contraction (W26 45, S26 63) YC reducing sizes, the agent category saturating within YC, or founders choosing alternatives over YC?

themes.title: Platform-vs-App Structure
themes.scope: The report analyzes the distribution of value across the work-agent market stack, comparing L1 runtimes, L2 build platforms, L3 vertical agents, L4 services, L5 incumbent suites, and X modalities as of 2026-09-09.
themes.headline: Value concentrates heavily at the application layer, with L3 holding roughly 60% of census-visible agent revenue and 67% of known $1B+ valuations.
findings: L3 vertical agents hold $2.96B in disclosed revenue across 34 companies, led by Cognition at ~$900M run-rate (Sept 2026).
L3 valuations peak at Cognition with $48B (2026-09-08), which is ~10x the L1 peak of Temporal at $5B (Feb 2026).
Visible funding is heavily skewed toward L3 at $22.3B, representing 74% of the $30.1B total visible funding.
L1 runtimes are priced on strategic position rather than cash flow, with Temporal ($5B) and Exa ($2.2B) disclosing no ARR.
Acquisition premiums favor proven work delivery, such as Salesforce-Fin at ~$3.6B for ~$100M agent ARR (Jun 2026).
L5 suites out-earn standalone platforms, with Salesforce Agentforce reporting $800M AI ARR (Sept 2026), exceeding combined L1 and L2 revenue of $532M.
X modality layer behaves like L1 in pricing but L3 in revenue, exemplified by ElevenLabs with $500M ARR and an $11B valuation (2026).
The agent-runtime layer (L1) has adopted a metered-utility pricing model similar to Cloudflare, with E2B pricing CPU at $0.000014-0.000112/vCPU-s.
The Cloudflare analogy breaks because enterprises buy outcomes (resolved tickets) rather than runtimes (sandbox-seconds).
L2 build platform valuations are often carried by adjacent-category heritage, such as Glean's $7.2B (Jun 2025) based on enterprise knowledge search.
Middle-layer (L2) instability is evidenced by exits into suites at single-digit billions, while L3 leaders raise at $10-48B.
L1 census-visible revenue is thin at $82M across 9 companies, while visible funding is $2.97B.
implications: Platform value resides in the binding and governance layer (data, integrations, memory) rather than the commoditizing metered-runtime slice.
Standalone L2 platforms without adjacent-category distribution are likely to be absorbed by suites or RPA incumbents.
The modality layer (X) is a unique value pool capable of pairing infrastructure-grade revenue with application-grade multiples.
New entrants can capture value in the outcome layer only through deep vertical integration of connectors and workflow knowledge.
open_questions: Is the low L1 revenue a result of pre-revenue scale or private non-disclosure by leaders like Temporal and OpenRouter?
Will the binding layer remain independent or be absorbed by MCP and suite control planes?
Does the platform layer's share of enterprise AI spend remain at ~2% or climb toward 15%?

themes.title: Cloud Marketplace AI Agents
themes.scope: Comprehensive research on how AI apps and agents are distributed across eight major marketplaces: Microsoft Azure, AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud, Salesforce, ServiceNow, OpenAI GPT Store, Hugging Face, and NVIDIA NGC. Covers catalog sizes, adoption signals, pricing models, protocol support, and competitive positioning as of 2026-09-10.
themes.headline: Eight AI agent marketplaces launched within 30 months, each as a distribution channel for its own platform; Microsoft Copilot Studio leads adoption with 230K orgs and 10M users, while Salesforce Agentforce reached $1.2B ARR and ServiceNow crossed $1B AI ACV.
findings: Eight marketplaces launched within 30 months: OpenAI GPT Store (Jan 2024), Salesforce AgentExchange (Mar 2025), AWS (Jul 2025), Microsoft (Sep 2025), ServiceNow (Jan 2026), Hugging Face Agent Hub (Mar 2026), Google (Apr 2026), and NVIDIA NGC evolving.
Microsoft Copilot Studio is the dominant platform by adoption: 230K organizations, 10M enterprise users, 2B tasks/month, 30M paid Copilot seats.

Salesforce Agentforce reached $1.2B ARR in under two years with 29K deals, 2.4B agentic work units, and 19T tokens processed; Flex Credits pricing at $0.10/action is the closest to per-outcome pricing on any marketplace.
ServiceNow crossed $1B AI ACV with 2,600 Now Assist customers and 9x growth in agentic deployments in 9 months; AI Control Tower governs agents across any system.
AWS launched with 900+ AI agent listings and Bedrock AgentCore (GA Oct 2025); 2M+ downloads; supports MCP and A2A; agents run in customer own AWS account.
Google has 56+ partner agents from 50+ publishers; 8M+ paid Gemini Enterprise seats; ~90% Fortune 100; $750M partner fund; best governance model with SPIFFE cryptographic agent identities.
OpenAI GPT Store has 3M+ GPTs created but only 159K active (5.3% survival rate); median creator income $47/month; enterprise business is $5B+ ARR with 1M+ business customers.
Hugging Face has 3M+ models, 1.3M Spaces, 13M users; Agent Hub launched March 2026 with ~8K agents; acquired by NVIDIA for $12.9B in August 2026.
NVIDIA NGC has 10,000+ models/containers, 100K+ NIM downloads; AI Enterprise at $4,500/GPU/year; AgentIQ for orchestration; deliberately avoids application layer.
Every big-vendor marketplace is a distribution channel for its own platform, not a neutral market; the agent price is never the whole price.
MCP is supported by 7 of 8 marketplaces; A2A is supported by AWS, Google, Salesforce, and ServiceNow but not OpenAI; Google adds UCP and AP2 protocols.
No marketplace offers per-outcome pricing (per-resolution, per-task-completed); Salesforce Flex Credits at $0.10/action is the closest.
The NVIDIA-Hugging Face acquisition creates a vertically integrated monopoly: GPUs, CUDA-X, NIM, AgentIQ, Nemotron models, and model distribution hub.

implications: The marketplace is a new layer in the agent stack, sitting between agent builders and enterprise buyers, adding procurement, governance, and deployment wrapping.
Distribution is concentrating at the platform layer that owns the marketplace; the marketplace operator captures rent on every agent sold through it.
Copilot Studio is the dominant enterprise agent platform by adoption; AWS leads on openness; Google leads on governance; Salesforce leads on per-action pricing.
The NVIDIA-Hugging Face acquisition creates a vertically integrated monopoly on the agent development lifecycle from silicon to model distribution.
Protocol convergence is happening around MCP (7 of 8 marketplaces); the A2A gap (OpenAI absent) is the key interoperability risk.
ServiceNow AI Control Tower is the only cross-platform agent governance tool that can govern agents from other marketplaces including Microsoft.
open_questions: How many agents are actually deployed in production through each marketplace? Listing counts are not deployment counts.
What is the revenue flowing through each marketplace for agent purchases? Neither Azure nor AWS discloses agent-specific GMV.
Will cross-marketplace portability emerge, or will vendor lock-in prevent agents from moving between platforms?
Will per-outcome pricing reach the marketplace, or will per-action (Salesforce Flex Credits) remain the closest approximation?
What happens to the NVIDIA-Hugging Face acquisition regulatory review, and how does it shape the open-source agent ecosystem?
